name: Marco Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, of course. I'm Marco, I'm 27, and I manage the cattle on a mixed farm owned by the Lind family. It's about 120 suckler cows, so cows that raise their own calves for beef, plus around eighty hectares of hay and silage and a bit of barley.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First thing, before I'm even out of bed, I check the app for the cattle collars. They're GPS collars that keep the cows inside a fence that only exists on the map, so I move the herd to fresh grass by dragging a line on my phone. Then I fly the drone over the far fields to count calves, because walking it takes two hours and the drone takes twelve minutes. Summer is all hay: mowing, turning, baling, and praying it doesn't rain. I like that the job is half cowman and half nerd, but the pay is honestly poor, and the hay season wipes me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask a chat assistant to sort the calving records, check withdrawal periods on medicines, and write the forms for the farm payments. My partner Noor is a nurse, and she laughs that I talk to my phone more than to her. We've got about three weeks of money saved, and there are hardly any cattle jobs within an hour of here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit of a let-down for me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still worth it, because they are. The collars alone save me two hours a day, and I'd keep telling the older farmers at the market that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd also be relieved for the people who are scared of it, because a lot of my mates in the pub aren't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what I use and try to get the Linds to put collars on the heifers too. I'd probably start charging neighbours to set up virtual fencing for them, maybe a hundred a farm, because nobody else round here knows how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored. Like a promised storm that only drizzles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone actually asked you to set up their fencing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two neighbours have already asked me, the Okonjos and old Mr Brandt. Mr Brandt can't use a smartphone, so I'd be on call for him, which is fine, he pays in eggs and gossip as much as money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with that extra money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it would go to savings, because three weeks isn't enough. The rest would go on a better drone, which Noor would say is the wrong answer.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are still worth it, because the collars alone save me two hours a day. I'd keep telling the older farmers at the market that.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, but relieved for the people who are scared of it. A lot of my mates in the pub aren't comfortable with this stuff like I am.
S0.do: Keeps using the collars, drone and chat assistant and pushes the farm to collar the heifers too. Starts charging neighbours about a hundred a farm to set up virtual fencing.
S0.feel: Calm and a little bored, like a storm that only drizzles.
S0.quote: Mr Brandt can't use a smartphone, so I'd be on call for him, which is fine, he pays in eggs and gossip as much as money.
S0.fieldNote: Marco already lives in the most AI-heavy corner of farming his budget allows, so a fizzle disappoints him. His instinct even in the calm picture is to turn his skills into a side income for neighbours. He thinks about people who are more frightened than he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on. That's the one I'm sort of preparing for already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small farms if we get the rules right, and a disaster if only the big operators can afford the kit. I'd post about public grants for shared machines and push the farmers' group to get organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well out of it, at least for a while. The people who can run the machines get more valuable, and I'm one of them, which is a bit uncomfortable to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Linds for a pay rise tied to the time I'm saving them, written down. I'd set up the fencing business properly, maybe with a second-hand quad and a trailer, and I'd look into leasing a robot mower for the hay with two neighbours, splitting the cost three ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit uneasy underneath. I know I'm on the lucky side of it, and I'm not sure that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a share in a robot mower with three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got almost nothing saved, so a lease would have to pay its way in the first hay season. I'd do the numbers with the chat assistant and then get the bank manager to check them, because I don't trust either one alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, who drives the baler for us in summer. He's fifty-five and he won't touch a screen. I'd try to get him on the robot side with me, but he'd probably tell me where to go.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for small farms if the rules are right and a disaster if only big operators can afford the kit. I'd push for public grants for shared machines.
S1.think: I think I'd do well out of it, at least for a while, because people who can run the machines become more valuable. That's a bit uncomfortable to say out loud.
S1.do: Asks his employer for a written pay rise tied to time saved and sets up the fencing business properly. Looks into leasing a robot mower for hay with two neighbours, checking the numbers with AI and the bank.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, uneasy underneath because he knows he's on the lucky side.
S1.quote: I'd do the numbers with the chat assistant and then get the bank manager to check them, because I don't trust either one alone.
S1.fieldNote: He moves first but carefully, testing AI's sums against a human banker. He admits he would benefit and finds that awkward given his views on fairness. His wish to bring an older colleague along is real, though he expects to be turned down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That changes everything I just said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loud and clear: the gains have to go to everyone, not just whoever owns the robots. I'd back a basic income, a payment from the government to every adult, and public ownership of the big AI systems, and I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my advantage vanishes. If the AI can run the collars and the drone and the hay robot itself, the Linds don't need a cowman who is good with phones. The skill I'm proud of has about eighteen months of value left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze everything I can out of the next two years: run the fencing business flat out, save every spare penny, and get the farmers' group to buy robots together so we at least own a piece of them. I'd join whatever campaign is pushing for the robot money to be shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And strangely grief-stricken, because I've spent five years getting good at the thing that eats itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said save every spare penny. What does that look like with three weeks in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. I've never had more than three weeks saved, and in two years I'd need much more than that. I don't know how we'd do it on my wage and Noor's, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Noor's job be safer than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my one hope. People still want a person when they're ill. But I've seen what these tools can do, and I'm not sure even she's safe.

S2.say: I'd say the gains must go to everyone, not just whoever owns the robots. I'd back a basic income and public ownership of the big AI systems everywhere I could.
S2.think: My advantage would vanish, because the AI could run the collars, drone and hay robot without me. The skill I'm proud of would have about eighteen months of value left.
S2.do: Runs the fencing side business flat out for two years and saves every spare penny. Pushes the local farmers' group to buy robots together and joins campaigns to share the gains.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and grieving for skills he spent years building.
S2.quote: I've spent five years getting good at the thing that eats itself.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture flips his position from winner to loser, and he sees it at once. Even with little money he reaches for shared ownership instead of going it alone. He was honest that he has no idea how to build savings fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to set up community ownership, so farms buy the robots together and the money stays local. I'd push for public money to help farmers' cooperatives do exactly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to switch from being the guy who uses the tools to the guy who runs a small robot service for the whole valley. If the AI does the farming, someone still has to own it, repair it and answer the phone when it breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start a short online course on farm robot maintenance, at night. In year two, with two or three neighbours, I'd set up a small cooperative to share a robot mower and baler. By year four I'd hope to be working for the cooperative instead of a single farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way. The kind of nerves you get before a big sale at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the cooperative doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least I'd have spent five years learning, not hiding, and I'd have something to take somewhere else. And I'd still want to keep a few cows of my own, just for the joy of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years enough to persuade farmers to share anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen three neighbours sit on a cooperative idea for ten years. If I had five, I'd need them to say yes in the first year, or I'd go ahead without them.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to set up community ownership so farms buy robots together and the money stays local. I'd push for public money for farmers' cooperatives.
S3.think: Five years is enough to switch from using the tools to running a small robot service for the whole valley. Someone still has to own it, fix it and answer the phone when it breaks.
S3.do: Starts an evening online course in farm robot maintenance this year and sets up a small cooperative with neighbours in year two to share a robot mower and baler. Aims to work for the cooperative by year four.
S3.feel: Anxious in a good way, like nerves before a big sale at the market.
S3.quote: If the AI does the farming, someone still has to own it, repair it and answer the phone when it breaks.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a business plan built on shared ownership. He is realistic that farmers are slow to agree and is ready to go ahead alone. He wants to keep a few cows for the pleasure of it, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, that sounds almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly: train people, share the machines, and make sure no one's left behind. I'd say it loudly at the farmers' meetings, because people hear ten years and think it means never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me to own something. A cooperative, a robot service, maybe even a few hectares and a herd, if land gets cheaper when the big farms automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the robot course in the first year, but I'd take the cooperative slower and get it right. Noor and I would start a proper savings plan, even fifty a week, and I'd keep the fencing business going to fund it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited about the next decade, a bit worried about people who won't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the people who won't move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah again. Ten years takes him to sixty-five, so he's probably fine. It's the forty-year-olds who think ten years is a long time who worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change any plans with Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd want kids in that decade, and I'd want them to grow up on a farm, even if robots do half the work.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly: train people, share the machines and leave no one behind. I'd say it loudly, because people hear ten years and think it means never.
S4.think: Ten years is enough for me to own something, like a cooperative, a robot service or even a small herd. Land might get cheaper if the big farms automate.
S4.do: Starts the robot course in year one, builds the cooperative slowly and keeps the fencing business to fund a savings plan of about fifty a week. Plans to have children with Noor and raise them on a farm.
S4.feel: Mostly calm and excited about the decade ahead, worried for people who won't move.
S4.quote: It's the forty-year-olds who think ten years is a long time who worry me.
S4.fieldNote: For Marco the long warning is an opportunity, possibly even a path to owning land. His worry moves from himself to middle-aged workers who will mistake ten years for never. His family plans grow rather than shrink in this picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It turns my best skills into nothing before I've saved a penny. What would help is grants for farmers' cooperatives to buy robots together, plus a basic income so the gains are shared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the whole question, really. If farmers and workers own a share, most of these pictures are fine. If they don't, none of them are.

headlineQuote: I've spent five years getting good at the thing that eats itself.
portrait: Marco is a 27-year-old cattle manager on a mixed beef and hay farm, living with his partner Noor, a nurse, on about three weeks of savings. He uses AI every day, from GPS cattle collars to a chat assistant for records, and he runs a small sideline setting up virtual fencing for neighbours. In the slower pictures he sees himself as one of the winners, and he's uncomfortable about it. The two-year picture alarms him because his hard-won skills would lose their value before he could save anything. Given five or ten years, he plans robot training and a shared robot cooperative, and he believes ownership decides who wins.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because it would turn his best skills into nothing before he had saved anything.
whatWouldHelp: Grants for farmers' cooperatives to buy robots together, plus a basic income so the gains are shared.
